June 2010 # Froth blown away - Fears over sovereign debt in Europe and the ensuing risk aversion saw investors flee to the relative safety of the US dollar. As a result, a fall in copper prices to almost $6,400/t on 20th May and a subsequent recovery to just $6,800-6,900/t at the time of writing has blown away most of the froth that had built up in late March and early April. - The upturn in consumption remains on track, with the usual seasonally stronger H1 demand pattern having re-emerged this year. China-led Asia remains well out in front of North America and Europe in terms of recovery. - There continue to be mixed responses to market developments, with some ploughing ahead with expansions while others remain cautious. We see the market moving into a deficit in Q2 that is driving a reduction in exchange warehouse stocks. This should support prices in the near term, barring any further macroeconomic shocks. |The supply/deman

Prices had already come off to about **copper demand** $7,400/t at the end of April. Subsequently, fears that **105** the debt crisis in Europe would lead to more stress on the international (particularly European) banking **100** system increased and led in turn to a flight to the safety of the US dollar. As a result, the euro sank and **95** dragged the copper price down with it. Copper fell below the $7,000/t mark on 5th May and then traded at **90 Copper 3-M Aluminium 3-M** around this level through 14th May. As the fears over **US dollar exchange rate** the fate of the European banking system grew, the **85** dollar strengthened further and the copper price slipped **Fears over demand outlook worsen - China: monetary policy tightening** below the $6,500/t level. The 3-month price fell to a - **default Greece: alert over sovereign debt 80** low of $6,424/t on 20th May, as the euro fell to a four- **Jan-10 Feb-10 Mar-10 Apr-10 May-10** year low of $1.21/€. With fears abating, prices have Data: LME, US Federal Reserve now recovered to trade at around $6,800-6,900/t on 27th May. The sell off has been strongly correlated with movements in the US dollar against most foreign currencies, which indicates a general aversion to risk. More evidence of risk aversion is that the decline in prices was not specific to copper, with all LME metals down over the past month. In fact, aluminium has closely tracked movements in copper since the start of the year. Uncertainty about the global economy has been driving prices recently. At the same time the copper market fundamentals appear to be holding up well and remain supportive for copper prices. In particular, the usual seasonal increase in consumption is coming through. As a result, we are forecasting that in Q2 the market will be in deficit by 173,000t. This is reflected in exchange stocks falling to below 740,000t by 20th May, almost 56,000t lower than their peak at the beginning of March. COMEX stocks are the notable exception, having stayed flat throughout April and May at just over 101,000t. SHF

E stocks rose to above 189,000t on 29<sup>th</sup> April, taking them to levels not seen since August 2002.  Subsequently, though, stocks in Chinese exchange warehouses have been on a downward trend, falling by about 21,000t to 168,000t as of 20<sup>th</sup> May.  The LME has led the way on exchange stock declines.  Drawdowns in the US, Europe and Asia totalled almost 28,000t between 26<sup>th</sup> April and 26<sup>th</sup> May, which we attribute mainly to increases in seasonal demand.  Some of the recent declines in the USA, however, have been due to rising freight rates making metal in the LME 

warehouses in New Orleans the cheaper option for nearby fabricators, rather than a general tightening of supply in the USA.  New Orleans currently accounts for 60% of LME warehouse stocks in the USA, which is down from 64% at its recent peak on 9<sup>th</sup> March.  New Orleans stocks have fallen by almost 25,000t since then, while LME stocks elsewhere in the country rose by over 5,000t. 

### **Consumption is holding up fairly well…** 

Demand for semi fabricated products continues to hold up well and is supporting refined consumption by the fabricators.  Asia remains the strongest performer, still led by China.  Strip and plate for electronic and electrical applications is seeing the strongest recovery, and this is evident across the world not just in Asia. Alloy rod, which is used extensively in construction applications, is doing better than many market participants feared, but tube production is still generally lagging overall semis production. 

Chinese refined consumption growth is still solid, although concerns about the rate of growth in Chinese cathode consumption in H2 of this year keep growing with each announcement of a further tightening of credit

policy.  We forecast that copper semis production in 2010 will grow by at least 10%.  Refined consumption growth is forecast to be higher than semis production, up by 11.5% for the year as a whole, as scrap availability remains below pre-crisis levels.  Refined growth is slightly lower than our previous forecast of 12%, due to the impact of the US anti-dumping case on tube exports and production.  We believe this growth in cathode consumption will be fed by a combination of higher domestic production, imports of at least 2.3Mt this year and a drawdown of unreported stocks.  Despite the tightening in credit availability, we expect orders for semis will remain robust in China, with any impact of the change in credit policy starting to be felt only in Q4 2010. 

We estimate that the rest of Asia saw refined consumption grow by 23% y-o-y in Q1, when comparisons were made with the depths of the downturn last year.  In Q2, we expect the rate of growth to decelerate to about 9% y-o-y.  Growth rates will decelerate further in H2 2010, as y-o-y comparisons are made with the recovery phase,

but will remain positive.  Japan is contributing the largest absolute tonnage increase and one of the largest percentage increases in refined consumption this year, as stimulus measures and export demand drive a recovery from the catastrophic declines seen last year.  Indian consumption of refined metal is benefiting from the solid economic recovery from last year’s wobble due to the financial crisis.  In India, unlike China, scrap availability is back to pre-crisis levels, which is dampening demand for cathode as semi-fabricators that can do so are taking cheaper scrap, in preference to cathode. 

North American consumption has hit bottom but is not showing a sustained V-shaped recovery.  Demand for semi fabricated products has increased, for example due to the restocking throughout the automotive supply chain following the collapse in auto output last year.  In addition, tube makers are seeing the benefit of increased orders following the preliminary anti-dumping duties imposed on Chinese and Mexican tube imports earlier in May.  However, at this stage the recovery is not broad based.  The construction market in the US will continue to be a drag on consumption growth.  Tax credits for homebuyers expired at the end of April, which prompted a flurry of buying that boosted existing home sales in the US to a five month high.  It seems that the higher sales have only led to more homeowners placing their property on the market, as the inventory of existing home sales rose in April to over 4 million or 8.4 months of inventory at the April selling rate, up from 8.1 months worth of inventory in March.  House prices are, therefore, likely to remain under pressure and constrain growth in the new home starts that would lead to higher copper consumption. 

In Europe the situation is a north-south divide.  Northern Europe is seeing good demand for semis, from exporters in particular, but Southern Europe is stuck in recession as the sovereign debt crisis and fiscal contraction sap demand.  This is leading to further measures to contain the damage to margins, as seen by General Cable permanently reducing the workforce at its Spanish operations.  We believe that Russia is likely to reintroduce the export duty on cathode, having already reintroduced a duty on nickel.  Last year rod production fell by 39% as net exports fell by almost 200,000t following the removal of the export duty.  CRU believes that the drop in exports last year was mostly to the Gulf States and North Africa via traders based in the Netherlands and Cyprus.  Assuming a reintroduction and higher rod production, the question is where will the wirerod end up?  As the Gulf is now more self-sufficient in rod production it will be difficult to place Russian rod here.  China would be a logical destination, but shipping costs largely rule this out.  As the nearest major market representing 14% of world wirerod consumption, Europe is exposed.  However, the eventual closure of Nexan’s Canadian rod mill

(which we now expect in Q4 this year) will open up an opportunity for some of the material to be shipped to North America. 

### **…with supply also remaining solid** 

Overall, we expect that refined production will again record almost no change from the 18.1Mt level recorded in both 2008 and 2009.  The response of producers to the downturn in demand and uncertainty over the recovery has been mixed.  Prices sustained at over $6,000/t since August last year have prompted a rethink by some producers of the viability of projects.  For example, MMG is ramping up its expansion of Sepon to

80,000t/y capacity from 65,000t/y, which it approved in October 2009.  In contrast, other miners remain cautious, with Rio Tinto having announced conservative guidance in its latest quarterly report of a decline in output this year compared to 2009 of over 100,000t. 

The brief strike at Collahuasi by contract workers over 7-11 May took out around 11,000t of refined production.  The potential significance of the strike is that it lays down a marker for Chilean producers on potential cost increases, as the vast majority of workers are on contract.  As almost all Q4 2009 results are in and most for Q1 2010, we have removed the remaining disruption allowance for 2009 and reduced the Q1 allowance.  As a result, our estimate of production in 2009 is now 64,000t higher than last month.  In Q1 2010 our reduced estimates of output (principally in Chile, Peru and Sweden) have more than offset increased estimates (mainly in China and the USA), leaving Q1 37,000t lower than presented in the May Monitor.  BHP Billiton has also just announced that Olympic Dam is on course to ramp back up to full capacity by end-June. 

### **Premia stable in Europe and US…** 

In the US, as mentioned above, freight costs continue to increase, reflecting overstretched trucking capacity. On the one hand, the cumulative impact of many smaller trucking companies having gone bankrupt over the past 18 months means total trucking capacity has been reduced.  In addition, the usual seasonal increase in demand for trucks to transport fruits and vegetables has tightened availability of trucks and raised freight rates. These higher rates are reflected in our estimate of the Northeast premium rising to 4.0-5.0¢/lb from 3.5-5.0¢/lb last month.  The rise is entirely down to the higher freight costs, as overall demand remains subdued. Premiums for the Midwest are slightly lower at around 4.25¢/lb and in the Gulf Coast down to 3.75¢/lb.  The draw down in stocks at the LME’s New Orleans warehouse is in part due to fabricators in the region finding it cheaper to buy warrants and ship metal to their operations rather than take delivery from traders. 

Overall, premiums in May were stable at $60-80/t in Europe.  There were a wide range of quotes in this month’s survey, with a bias to the high side indi

cating that premiums may move higher if spot demand continues to increase. One anomaly though, is that Southern Europe is seeing higher spot demand and premia, which is reportedly due in part to KGHM selling less spot material following their recently announced contract to sell 5,000t/m to NKT Cable. ### **…but heading higher in China as arb. re-opens** With the re-opening of the SHFE-LME arbitrage window, Chinese premiums for imported cathode rose back up to $80-100/t in the last couple of weeks. Domestic supply is still plentiful in China, as domestic refined production continues to increase by double digit figures. With imports having only fallen 8% m-o-m in April, we expect that imports will come off again in May. However, the new scrap import regulations we have mentioned over the last few issues of the Monitor are coming into force on 1st June and are likely to lead to slightly lower scrap imports and increased refined offtake. We see Chinese refined imports at a minimum of 150,000t/m reflecting the level of contract business, which provides the new floor for monthly imports. Meanwhile, the open SHFE-LME arbitrage will lead to higher imports in the coming months. China, even with galloping refined production increases, remains structurally short of copper and will remain a net importer. The risk remains that off warrant drawdowns may increase if LME prices tumble as the speculative holders of this metal need to liquidate their holdings to meet other financial obligations. ### **Prices more in line with fundamentals but remain hostage to events** We believe that the froth has been essentially been removed off copper prices and we anticipate that now it will be the fundamentals which will provide price direction. All of these sectors are reasonably concentrated - especially upstream, where there are less than ten dominant companies. The major mining and refining companies are Mineraзгo Caraнba, Paranapanema, Vale and Yamana Gold. Going further downstream, there are 17 wirerod producers and over 100 wire and cable manufacturers in Brazil. The largest copper semis producers in Brazil are Cecil, Ibrame, Paranapanema and Termomecanica. Copper semis production was 329,000t in 2009, compared to 388,000t in 2008. This is forecast to total 354,000t in 2010, of which 142,000t will be semimanufactured products and 212,000t will be wire and cable products, according to Sindicel. This data is generally reliable, but one should be aware that it also tends to underreport output of smaller size companies or those that only produce for internal use. In terms of trade, Brazil is a net importer of copper products. In 2009, the country imported 15,000t of brass mill products and 22,000t of wirerod. For the same year, it exported 14,000t of brass mill products and 20,000t of wirerod. ## **Drivers of the Brazilian copper market** We estimate that Brazilian refined copper consumption will be 335,000t in 2010, an 14.3% increase y-o-y. The country’s GDP fell by 0.2% y-o-y in 2009 and is expected to grow by 5.7% y-o-y in 2010. We believe that the main drivers for copper demand in the short to medium term would be the national expenditure on infrastructure and a strong automotive sector. The Brazilian government previously announced a growth acceleration program (PAC 1) for the period 2007-2010, with US$31B allocated to logistics (including the construction of roads, railways, ports, airports and hydroways); US$153B to be spent on electrical energy development and US$95B budgeted for social and urban investments. A project to connect the northern and southern Brazilian transmission and distribution grids should stimulate demand for power cables and overhead conductors, which means demand for wirerod and wire and cable is going to be robust throughout this year. PAC 2 of the program focuses on housing and energy for 2011-2014. Currently, the country has a deficit of 6M houses. Housing sales are predicted to grow 15.7% in 2010. An extra US$33B will be invested in building works related to the international events including the FIFA World Cup in 2014 and the Olympic G

# Industry News 

## **Production** 







- On Friday 7<sup>th</sup> May, a group of contractors’ workers at **Collahuasi** (Chile) took over the mine facilities by blocking access bringing operations to a halt.  The contractors were protesting over narrowing of the differences in their treatment compared to company employees.  Their demands include higher salaries, to receive end-of-conflict bonuses (to which they are not legally entitled whilst directly and unionised workers are) and better working conditions, including improvements to the standards of the contractors' camp.  The protest ended on Tuesday 11<sup>th</sup> May, when the police intervened in what was declared an illegal strike and the next day the company declared _force majeure_ to clients.  A week later operations were back at full production and the _force majeure_ was lifted.  The company declared a production loss of 41,500t of copper concentrates, which CRU estimates contain around 11,000t of copper-in-concentrate using the average copper concentrates grade (27%) of Collahuasi’s concentrates exports in Q1 2010.  In 2010, Collahuasi was expected to produce 393,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 35,000t of EW copper cathode. 

- On May 2<sup>nd</sup> it was announced that **Australia’s** government is planning to impose a **40% tax on profits** generated from mining in the country from 2012.  A number of miners, including **Rio Tinto** and **BHP Billiton** , responded with dismay and are questioning the possible effects on the Australian mining industry competitiveness.  The proposed Resource Super-Profits Tax comes in response to a series of recommendations made by the Treasury Secretary Ken Henry at the end of last year, following a complete review of Australia’s taxation system. (The recommendations to the government were only made public recently.)  Around 886,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 43,000t of EW copper cathode are expected to be produced in Australia in 2010. 

- On 4<sup>th</sup> May it was announced that Polish miner **KGHM** has signed an agreement to form a joint venture with Canadian-listed **Abacus Mining & Exploration Corporation** to develop Abacus’ **Afton-Ajax** copper-gold project, located in British Columbia. According to the agreement, KGHM is to invest US$37M in the project to finance the completion of a Bankable Feasibility Study (BFS), in return for a 51% stake in the project.  The agreement also includes an option for KGHM to acquire a further 29% interest in the project on completion of the BFS. CRU currently characterises this project as “possible”, with a likely start-up year of 2015.  Production is expected to be 48,000t/y of copperin-concentrate at full capacity. 



- On 14<sup>th</sup> May, **Lundin Mining** reported that management and the workers’ union at its **Neves Corvo** underground copper-zinc mine in Portugal have reached an agreement on a new pay-for-performance

based incentive that has been endorsed by the workforce. The union had previously notified the operator, Lundin, on 20<sup>th</sup> April of its intention to hold a strike between 5<sup>th</sup> May and 12<sup>th</sup> May.  The strike was subsequently called off. Earlier in the year, employees had held two hour strikes at the beginning of each shift between February and April. Lundin have advised that around 5,000t less copper-in-concentrate will be produced in 2010 due to the labour disruptions, and Neves Corvo is now expected to produce 77,000t of copper-in-concentrates this year. 



- In late May, **Quadra Mining** and **FNX** completed the merger of the two companies that was announced in March.  The new company will be called **Quadra FNX Mining** .  The deal values the new company at around US$1.5B.  The merger will give Quadra shareholders 52% of the company and the remaining 48% to FNX shareholders.  In 2010, Quadra Mining’s mines ( **Robinson** and

**Carlota** in the USA; and **Franke** in Chile) are expected to produce a combined total of 49,000t of EW cathode and 61,000t of copper-in-concentrate. FNX is a Canadian nickel-copper-PGM producer and in 2010 is expected to produce 20,000t of contained copper in nickel concentrate. 



- On 25<sup>th</sup> May, **Ivanhoe Australia** announced that they have entered into significant strategic acquisition of **Barrick’s Osborne** copper-gold mine in Australia.  Ivanhoe Australia’s plans to develop their Merlin molybdenite-rhenium project and process its ore at Osborne’s facilities.  The consideration for the acquisition is A$17.4M (~US$14.4M) cash payment, 2% Net Smelter Returns Royalty capped at A$15M  (~US$12.5M) from ore extracted from the Osborne tenements only, and the assumption of all site environmental obligations including the provision of A$18.4M (~US$15.3M)  EPA Financial Assurance.  The settlement for the acquisition is scheduled for 30<sup>th</sup> September 2010.  In 2010, the last year of operation under the current mine plan, Osborne is expected to produce 21,000t of copper-in-concentrate. 

## **Exploration and Development** 









- On 24<sup>th</sup> May, **Citadel Resources** announced that the Exploitation (mining) Licence for their **Jabal Sayid** copper-gold project in Saudi Arabia had been granted. Jabal Sayid would be Saudi Arabia’s first base metals mine and CRU expects it to start-up in 2011 and produce 60,000t/y of copper-inconcentrate at full capacity. 

- On 18<sup>th</sup> May, it was reported that **Newmont Mining** is expecting to open their **Conga** gold-copper mine by late 2014.  Conga is located in northern Peru and is expected to produce between 72,000t/y and 95,000t/y of contained copper at full production. 

- **Codelco** reported that authorities had approved the environmental impact study for an open pit project at **El Teniente** (t

he world’s largest underground copper mine). The company’s board still needs to approve the investment (estimated at US$179M).  Operations would start-up in 2012 with a maximum processing capacity of 20,000t/d.  In addition, Codelco is also evaluating the “New Mine Level” project, which requires an investment of around US$1.6B and a 7-year construction period. In 2010, El Teniente would produce 363,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 12,000t of EW cathode. 

- On 26<sup>th</sup> May, it was reported that production at **BHP Billiton’s Olympic Dam** mine in Australia would return to normal this week after an accident seven months ago that reduced production by 75%.  In 2010, Olympic Dam is expected to produce 148,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 15,000t of EW cathode. 

## **Smelting and Refining** 





- **Boliden** announced at the end of April plans to increase its electronic scrap recycling capacity from the current level of 45,000t/y to 120,000t/y. Work on the expansion at the **Rцnnskдr** smelter in Sweden will take place over the next two years and a new Kaldo furnace, steam boiler, gas purification equipment and materials processing facilities are expected to be commissioned at the end of 2011 or beginning of 2012. The project is expected to cost SEK1.3B (~US$174M).
